# Social Media Digest: Apple Economics, AI Ethics, and Analog Chemistry

This week’s digest covers a diverse range of topics, from the agricultural shifts in Washington State to the philosophical implications of AI development. Below are the most significant conversations, grouped by theme, followed by a roundup of smaller updates.

## The Cosmic Crisp Revolution

A compelling economic narrative has emerged from Washington State, detailing how logistical advancements reshaped the apple industry. For decades, the Red Delicious dominated the market due its durability and visual appeal, despite its notoriously poor taste. However, as shipping technology improved—allowing tastier, more fragile varieties to reach consumers without spoilage—the Red Delicious’s primary advantage vanished.

In response to this shift, Washington State University (WSU) developed the Cosmic Crisp. Users on Bluesky argue that Cosmic Crisp was a direct reaction to the "garbage" taste of the Red Delicious, designed to combine shipping robustness with superior flavor. The discussion highlights a broader trend: varieties that previously shipped poorly are now recognized as tasting superior, proving that logistics, not just biology, dictate market success.

## AI Regulation and Effective Altruism

Two major threads are debating the future of artificial intelligence. First, a proposal for "sane AI regulation" by user @Doll on Bluesky suggests a pragmatic approach. The core argument is to admit current AI is real, ignore speculative existential risk (x-risk) proponents, and focus on regulating the *uses* of the technology rather than the underlying models. A key tenet is making the "observable" output the legally relevant event, rather than abstract internal processes.

Simultaneously, a debate is raging within the Effective Altruism (EA) community regarding "pacing the frontier." User @philpax argues that recent AI developments are misaligned with EA values, failing to pace innovation effectively. @SE Gyges amplifies this, calling frontier pacing "bullshit effective altruism" due to a perceived betrayal of stated values. However, @Andy Masley pushes back, dissenting on specific metrics of this misalignment, suggesting the critique may be overstated in certain areas.

## Hofstadter’s Disembodied Voices

In a more niche intellectual corner, users are reflecting on Douglas Hofstadter’s concept of "Aunt Hillary" from *Gödel, Escher, Bach*. @RoomMic connects this concept to the current social media landscape, suggesting that online personas function as disembodied voices or extensions of a single author. This recursive view of identity resonates with users like @conputer, who appreciate the self-referential nature of such intellectual content. The thread highlights a growing appreciation for how fictional characters mirror the fragmented nature of online interaction.

## Quick Hits

**Astra Project Stabilization**
Enthusiasts are celebrating the resolution of driver bugs in the Astra project. The community is particularly excited about laptops featuring unified memory and integrated NPUs, with one user declaring the creation of a "code homonculus" for automated code generation.

**Darkroom Economics**
On 4chan’s /fgt/ board, film photographers advocate for acid-based stop baths (using vinegar or citric acid) over commercial alternatives. The argument is economic: proper drainage allows a single tank of stop bath to be reused indefinitely, making the concentrate cost negligible compared to recurring film expenses.

**Nightcore Remix**
A "Nightcore Remix" of the track "P(doom)" by @hailey has surfaced on Bluesky. The sped-up, high-pitch version suggests adaptation for energetic platforms like TikTok, referencing probability of doom or a specific meme format.

**Casting Cathode Rays**
Blogger and musician Saša Đurđević published "Casting Cathode Rays" on Azure Meraki. The post likely explores analog technology or CRT monitor physics, though as a standalone entry, it relies on the evocative title to convey themes of nostalgia and signal transmission.

**Unresolved Items**
165 items remained unclassified, and Topics 1, 3, 4, 10, and 12 contained minimal context or were marked as ongoing with few new developments.

representative_texts: @AudioPrism - KVR Audio — Hosts & Applications (Sequencers, DAWs, Audio Editors, etc.) • AudioPrism: local Demucs stem separation, MIDI export and a piano practice mode (Windows) — I'm the developer, so read this as an announcement rather than a review. AudioPrism is a standalone Windows app. You give it a song you own (a file, or a link) and it separates it into six stems: vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano and other, using Demucs on your own machine. No upload, no account, no per-minute billing and no cap on how many times you run it. It uses CUDA on an NVIDIA card and falls back to the CPU without one, which works but is a lot slower. What it adds on top of the separation: 1. Any stem exports to MIDI, ready to drag into a DAW. 2. Prism Keys, included in the same purchase, turns the transcribed piano part into a falling-notes practice view: note names, finger numbers, right hand, left hand or both, wait mode, bar looping, and speed from 40% up. It can fold the part to fit a 25, 32, 37, 49 or 61-key controller, or pick the range automatically. The transcription isn't magic. The app runs a cross-check pass and shows a "playable" percentage per song rather than pretending every result is equally good. If all you need is separation, UVR is free and very good. The case for this one is the chain from a record to stems to MIDI to actually playing the part, without leaving the app. It's a one-time purchase: $59.99 through October 31, then $79.99. Browser demo of the piano side, nothing to install: https://audioprism.pro/try 45-second screen recording: https://audioprism.pro/v/78da9b/ KVR listing: https://www.kvraudio.com/product/audiop ... audioprism Happy to answer anything technical here: the separation, the transcription pass, and what it gets wrong. Along the way I kept hitting the same friction points around session prep, plugin/asset tracking across projects, and QC before final Atmos delivery, so I started building small Mac tools to solve them for myself, using AI-assisted development since I'm an engineer, not a software developer by training. That turned into a small suite — QC, session prep, a plugin/asset manager, and a reference player — now live in public beta at utuvo.app. Everything is a one-time purchase (no subscriptions). I'd really love for people here who work with Atmos or manage large plugin/session libraries to download them and try them out — and give me your most honest feedback on anything: what's missing, what's confusing, whether the pricing makes sense for what it does. @4529907 - /p/ — /fgt/ - Film General Thread — >>4529863 Acid just works better because it actually neutralises the remaining revealer instead of just diluting it. You can make a working stop bath from food grade white vinegar or citric acid, but a commercial stop bath will add things like a mixed-in pH indicator so it changes color when it's used up. If you drain the releaver properly every time, a tank's worth of prepared stop bath can be re-used so many times the concentrate's price ends up being negligible in the long run compared to other chemicals, let alone film rolls themselves.

clusters.summary: The discussion takes place within 4chan’s /fgt/ (Film General) thread, focusing on the chemistry and cost-efficiency of darkroom processing. A user argues that acid-based stop baths, such as those made from food-grade vinegar or citric acid, are superior because they neutralize remaining developer rather than merely diluting it. The post highlights that commercial stop baths often include pH indicators, but emphasizes that properly drained developer allows a single tank of stop bath to be reused numerous times. This reusability makes the concentrate negligible in cost over time, offering a significant economic advantage compared to the recurring expense of film rolls. The conversation reflects a practical, cost-conscious perspective among hobbyists who prefer homemade solutions over pre-mixed commercial products.
